name: Rafie Faruq

education.notes: Start/end years inferred from typical UK undergrad timing and known later milestones (trader job 2012, MSc 2016).
Won a CS prize among all MSc students; thesis on generative AI applied to structured legal text — predates the public GPT moment by ~5 years.

keyDecisions: Chose philosophy + economics rather than CS — kept a reasoning-and-incentives lens before going technical.
Picked LSE specifically — optimised for the finance recruiting pipeline rather than tech.
lessons: A non-CS undergrad doesn't block a deep-tech founding path if you re-enter via a quantitative masters later.
Optimise your undergrad for the next step you actually want — for him, that was a London trading desk, not a CS career.

keyDecisions: Took a high-paying graduate finance job — bought himself runway and credibility before founding.
Used the day job to fund the night project — explicit hustler pattern rather than dropping out at 22.
Quit at 26 to retrain rather than stack two more years of bonus — refused the golden-handcuff trap.
lessons: A trader role builds tolerance for asymmetric risk and rapid decision-making under uncertainty — directly useful for founding.
Day-job runway lets you build a serious side project without burning savings or signing bad SAFE terms.
Bank salaries are an option you should exercise then exit — staying past the second bonus is usually a value-destroying trade.
careerSteps.notes: Years estimated from interview accounts that he worked by day at a Japanese investment bank while building a side business by night. Comp range is a UK trader-band estimate, not directly confirmed.

keyDecisions: Picked a project that could go viral without paid acquisition — chose distribution-first design.
Built with a flatmate — minimised coordination cost when the day job was eating most of his bandwidth.
Wound it down rather than forcing it into a venture — kept it as a learning, not an identity.
lessons: A successful-but-small side project (10k users, £50k donations) is a credential — proves you can ship and grow without proving you have to commit to that idea.
Side projects work best when you can pull the plug guilt-free — wedded-to-it side projects become bad founderships.
Pick side projects with viral mechanics so your scarcity resource (time) isn't also the growth lever.
careerSteps.notes: Reported reach: ~10,000 users, ~£50,000 raised for charity.

keyDecisions: Left a trader salary to re-skill into ML — explicit bet on AI before it was obvious (pre-Transformer, pre-GPT).
Chose a thesis on generative AI applied to legal contracts — vertical-specific, not generic.
Picked UCL specifically — adjacent to the London EF pipeline he would join immediately after.
lessons: Going back to a one-year technical masters in your mid-20s is a high-leverage reset if it lines you up with a forming wave.
Pick a thesis topic that doubles as a startup hypothesis — the year of research becomes a year of free customer-discovery.
Reset moves are cheaper than they look — one year of foregone bank comp is the price of a decade of right-wave positioning.
careerSteps.notes: Won a CS prize across the MSc cohort. Met co-founder Nitish Mutha during the MSc — both specialised in deep learning and NLP, programme taught in conjunction with Google DeepMind.

careerSteps.company: Genie AI (via Entrepreneur First, EF cohort EF9)
keyDecisions: Joined Entrepreneur First (Europe's talent-investor model) rather than bootstrapping alone — replaced a missing co-founder network with a structured one.
Started in 2017 — generative AI applied to legal, years before LLMs went mainstream. Held the conviction through pre-LLM 'cold winter' (2018-2022) when the field looked unsexy.
Stuck with the same vertical (legal contracts) for years — earned the right to ride the 2023+ LLM wave with existing domain trust and data.
Raised £13.3M Series A in Oct 2024 led by Google Ventures with Khosla Ventures participating — chose a strategic lead (GV) over a generalist for the post-LLM regulatory landscape.
lessons: Conviction in a wave before it is obvious is mostly a function of having technical skin in the game (the MSc thesis) — not vibes.
Vertical AI > horizontal AI for non-incumbents: pick a regulated, document-heavy vertical (law) where domain trust is the moat once the model commodity arrives.
Talent-investor programmes (EF) are a viable substitute for a strong existing co-founder network — especially in Europe where YC's network effects don't fully reach.
Surviving the trough between thesis and wave is the actual edge — most founders who chose generative AI in 2017 quit before 2022.
careerSteps.notes: EF9 cohort Oct 2017 - Mar 2018. Genie AI co-founded Nov 2017. Raised £2M seed (Jul 2019), then £13.3M Series A (Oct 2024) led by Google Ventures with Khosla Ventures participating. Genie AI reports 130,000+ companies using the platform with ~250 new companies joining daily as of recent press. Co-founder Nitish Mutha (CTO) met during the UCL MSc Machine Learning programme.

outcomes.currentStatus: Co-founder & CEO of Genie AI, a legal-AI agent for in-house lawyers and business professionals. No exit; equity value paper-only.

lessons.lesson: Cross-pollinate skills from one industry (trading: pricing, risk, speed) into an underserved vertical (legal) to find a disruptive angle.
lessons.source: inferred from Tech Funding News and Fintech Times interviews

lessons.lesson: Use a high-paying job as runway for a serious side project rather than dropping out prematurely.
A one-year quantitative masters in your mid-20s is a credible reset path into deep tech.
Pick the wave (generative AI) before it is consensus, and stay in your vertical long enough for the wave to arrive.
Entrepreneur First is the European structural substitute for YC — especially valuable if your existing network is finance-not-tech.
